This composition was chosen to narrow the candidate systems based on high-Z material requirements to minimize sputtering and low-activation elements to reduce radiotoxicity.
answers.conditions: Synthesized via magnetron sputtering; irradiated with 1-MeV Kr+2 up to 8 dpa
answers.measurement_outcome: Single-phase BCC structure; no sign of irradiation-created defects observed up to 8 dpa
answers.mechanism: Selection of W, Ta, V, and Cr based on high-Z properties and low-activation criteria to mitigate sputtering and radiotoxicity while avoiding intermetallic formation.
answers.boundary_limitation: The selection of elements was narrowed based on criteria excluding Ni, Cu, Al, Mo, Co, Nb, Fe, and Mn.
evidence_spans: In this work, we have developed a quaternary nanocrystalline W-Ta-V-Cr alloy that we have characterized under thermal conditions and after irradiation. Note that the possible combination of elements to synthesize an HEA is exceedingly large. To narrow the possible candidate systems, we have to bear in mind that high-Z materials are generally desirable to minimize sputtering. In addition, low-activation elements must be considered to reduce radiotoxicity, which excludes the use of Ni, Cu, Al, Mo, Co, or Nb. Furthermore, Fe and Mn usually form intermetallics, which might induce a more complex behavior. Thus, W, Ta, V, and Cr were chosen as testing ingredients for the target system. We show how this alloy can be synthesized using a magnetron sputtering deposition system. Both energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) analysis, which measures chemical composition, and atom probe tomography (APT) indicate W and Ta enrichment in the deposited films. The EDS mapping on both surface and cross-sectional areas and x-ray diffraction (XRD) results show a single-phase BCC after deposition. The samples were irradiated with 1-MeV Kr +2 in situ at the Intermediate Voltage Electron Microscope (IVEM)–Tandem Facility at Argonne National Laboratory up to 8 displacements per atom (dpa) with no sign of irradiation-created defects. Moreover, nanoindentation tests were also performed, showing hardness of the film on the order of ~15 GPa.

source_evidence_spans: Are high-entropy alloys the solution to radiation damage?

evidence_spans: In this work, we have developed a quaternary nanocrystalline W-Ta-V-Cr alloy that we have characterized under thermal conditions and after irradiation. Note that the possible combination of elements to synthesize an HEA is exceedingly large. To narrow the possible candidate systems, we have to bear in mind that high-Z materials are generally desirable to minimize sputtering. In addition, low-activation elements must be considered to reduce radiotoxicity, which excludes the use of Ni, Cu, Al, Mo, Co, or Nb. Furthermore, Fe and Mn usually form intermetallics, which might induce a more complex behavior. Thus, W, Ta, V, and Cr were chosen as testing ingredients for the target system. The samples were irradiated with 1-MeV Kr +2 in situ at the Intermediate Voltage Electron Microscope (IVEM)–Tandem Facility at Argonne National Laboratory up to 8 displacements per atom (dpa) with no sign of irradiation-created defects. Moreover, nanoindentation tests were also performed, showing hardness of the film on the order of ~15 GPa.
